from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import json

OUT = Path("/mnt/data/meridian_run_145/zoo_atlas")
OUT.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Near-aligned filament family: same interval carrier, changing
#    tangent misalignment. This is a geometry diagnostic only.
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
p = 0.16
s = np.linspace(0, 4*np.pi, 1200)
radii = [0.55, 0.10, 0.02]
align_rows = []

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(7.5, 6.2))
ax = fig.add_subplot(111, projection="3d")
for i, R in enumerate(radii):
    G = np.column_stack([R*np.cos(s) + 1.4*(i-1), R*np.sin(s), p*s])
    ax.plot(G[:,0], G[:,1], G[:,2], label=f"R={R:g}")
    kappa = R/(R*R+p*p)
    torsion = p/(R*R+p*p)
    tangent_angle = np.arctan2(R, p)
    align_rows.append({
        "radius": R,
        "pitch_parameter": p,
        "curvature": kappa,
        "torsion": torsion,
        "tangent_misalignment_rad": tangent_angle,
        "tangent_misalignment_deg": np.degrees(tangent_angle),
        "carrier_topology": "interval",
    })
ax.set_xlabel("x (display offset)")
ax.set_ylabel("y")
ax.set_zlabel("history/axis")
ax.set_title("Near-alignment is geometric, not a carrier-topology change")
ax.legend()
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig(OUT/"near_aligned_filament_family.png", dpi=220)
fig.savefig(OUT/"near_aligned_filament_family.svg")
plt.close(fig)

align_df = pd.DataFrame(align_rows)
align_df.to_csv(OUT/"near_aligned_filament_numeric.csv", index=False)

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Short high-curvature open segment with explicit fixed endpoints.
#    We do not assign a knot type: boundary/framing convention remains
#    a separate datum.
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
Rq, pq = 0.15, 0.03
sq = np.linspace(-0.75*np.pi, 0.75*np.pi, 600)
Q = np.column_stack([Rq*np.cos(sq), Rq*np.sin(sq), pq*sq])

q_kappa = Rq/(Rq*Rq+pq*pq)
q_tau = pq/(Rq*Rq+pq*pq)
q_speed = np.sqrt(Rq*Rq+pq*pq)
q_length = q_speed*(sq[-1]-sq[0])
q_chord = np.linalg.norm(Q[-1]-Q[0])
q_turn = (sq[-1]-sq[0])/(2*np.pi)

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(7.2, 6.0))
ax = fig.add_subplot(111, projection="3d")
ax.plot(Q[:,0], Q[:,1], Q[:,2], label="open segment")
ax.scatter([Q[0,0],Q[-1,0]],[Q[0,1],Q[-1,1]],[Q[0,2],Q[-1,2]], label="fixed endpoints")
ax.set_xlabel("x")
ax.set_ylabel("y")
ax.set_zlabel("history/axis")
ax.set_title("Short high-curvature open filament with explicit endpoints")
ax.legend()
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig(OUT/"bounded_high_curvature_segment.png", dpi=220)
fig.savefig(OUT/"bounded_high_curvature_segment.svg")
plt.close(fig)

q_df = pd.DataFrame([{
    "radius": Rq,
    "pitch_parameter": pq,
    "curvature": q_kappa,
    "torsion": q_tau,
    "arc_length": q_length,
    "endpoint_chord": q_chord,
    "turns": q_turn,
    "boundary_convention": "endpoints explicitly marked; tangent/framing not fixed",
    "topological_label": "UNRESOLVED",
}])
q_df.to_csv(OUT/"bounded_high_curvature_numeric.csv", index=False)

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Phase ripple as a field on a straight carrier, not displacement.
#    gamma(z) is unchanged. A normal director d(z,t) carries phase.
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
z = np.linspace(0, 1, 500)
k = 3
t0 = 0.17
omega_phase = 1.9
phase = 2*np.pi*k*z - omega_phase*t0
carrier = np.column_stack([np.zeros_like(z), np.zeros_like(z), z])
director = np.column_stack([np.cos(phase), np.sin(phase), np.zeros_like(z)])

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(7.3, 6.2))
ax = fig.add_subplot(111, projection="3d")
ax.plot(carrier[:,0], carrier[:,1], carrier[:,2], label="carrier centerline")
idx = np.linspace(0, len(z)-1, 28, dtype=int)
scale = 0.13
for ii in idx:
    base = carrier[ii]
    tip = base + scale*director[ii]
    ax.plot([base[0],tip[0]],[base[1],tip[1]],[base[2],tip[2]])
ax.set_xlabel("normal x")
ax.set_ylabel("normal y")
ax.set_zlabel("carrier coordinate")
ax.set_title("Phase field on a fixed carrier: centerline does not ripple")
ax.legend()
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig(OUT/"phase_field_on_fixed_carrier.png", dpi=220)
fig.savefig(OUT/"phase_field_on_fixed_carrier.svg")
plt.close(fig)

# Regression checks:
centerline_displacement = np.max(np.linalg.norm(carrier[:,:2], axis=1))
director_norm_error = np.max(np.abs(np.linalg.norm(director, axis=1)-1))
phase_advance = phase[-1]-phase[0]
phase_df = pd.DataFrame([{
    "phase_wavenumber_integer": k,
    "snapshot_time": t0,
    "phase_angular_frequency": omega_phase,
    "net_phase_advance_rad": phase_advance,
    "net_phase_advance_over_2pi": phase_advance/(2*np.pi),
    "max_centerline_transverse_displacement": centerline_displacement,
    "max_director_norm_error": director_norm_error,
    "object_type": "phase/director field on fixed carrier",
}])
phase_df.to_csv(OUT/"phase_field_numeric.csv", index=False)

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# Typed source-facing atlas: only fields supported by the historical Zoo
# are filled; unknowns stay unknown.
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
atlas_rows = [
    ["electron", "persistent filament", "twist handedness/loop/coupling mentioned generically", "longer singly curved; stable angular deviation", "baseline lepton resonance state", "independent", "persistent", "historical Zoo"],
    ["muon/tau", "persistent filament", "same broad lepton framing family", "tighter curve and/or faster twist mentioned", "heavier harmonic / resonance mode", "independent", "persistent but unstable", "historical Zoo"],
    ["neutrino", "persistent/possibly open filament", "possibly leaky/open-ended; not fixed", "near-aligned / near-parallel", "not separately fixed", "non-composite", "persistent/coherent", "historical Zoo"],
    ["quark", "short filament segment", "topology-dependent boundary constraints; color as phase/braid parity", "short, high-curvature/high-angle", "flavor = resonance mode", "must bind into composite in source", "persistent constituent", "historical Zoo"],
    ["photon", "ripple/transition on filament bundle", "not fixed", "carrier geometry not itself displaced by definition", "phase-alignment ripple", "travels along aligned bundles", "transient propagation", "historical Zoo"],
    ["gluon", "internal ripple mode", "braid context implied", "not fixed", "internal ripple/phase mode", "confined within braided quark thread", "transient/confined", "historical Zoo"],
    ["W/Z", "local reconfiguration event", "not fixed", "steep angular transition", "high-energy transition", "mediates/reconfigures", "short-lived event", "historical Zoo"],
    ["Higgs", "stabilization/structural event", "not fixed", "not fixed", "structural ripple/stabilization", "supports stable configurations", "event", "historical Zoo"],
    ["proton/neutron", "three-filament composite", "three-braid; twist compatibility", "bundle geometry", "internal modes not uniquely fixed", "3 braided quark filaments", "persistent composite", "historical Zoo"],
    ["pion/kaon/meson", "two-constituent bundle", "looped tension exchange mentioned", "short bundle", "not fixed", "quark-antiquark pair", "unstable composite", "historical Zoo"],
]
atlas = pd.DataFrame(atlas_rows, columns=["label","C_carrier","F_framing_topology","G_geometry","E_excitation","B_binding","P_persistence","source_scope"])
atlas.to_csv(OUT/"particle_zoo_typed_atlas_v0.csv", index=False)

manifest = {
    "near_alignment":{"pitch_parameter":p,"radii":radii},
    "bounded_segment":{"R":Rq,"p":pq,"s_range":[float(sq[0]),float(sq[-1])]},
    "phase_field":{"k":k,"t0":t0,"omega_phase":omega_phase},
    "status":"sandboxed diagnostic; not particle-parameter fit"
}
(OUT/"atlas_manifest.json").write_text(json.dumps(manifest,indent=2))

print("Near-alignment diagnostic:")
print(align_df.to_string(index=False))
print("\nBounded segment diagnostic:")
print(q_df.to_string(index=False))
print("\nPhase-field diagnostic:")
print(phase_df.to_string(index=False))
print("\nAtlas rows:", len(atlas))

### Meridian — Run 145 production pass

**Two-rate recurrence:** 🟢 the exact machinery survives. The lag discriminant is exact and the standalone code reproduces the benchmark with an answer-blind \(L_\*=30\). Under the frozen acquisition/noise configuration, \(\Delta\omega=0.10\) is strong at **0.69% median relative error**, \(0.03\) is 🟡 at **9.25%**, and \(0.01/0.003\) are ❌ not reliably resolved. The paper now correctly describes the numerical estimator as structured **OLS**, not TLS. RevTeX compiled, rendered, and was visually inspected.

**Particle Zoo:** the first substantial result survives and sharpens. The original Zoo makes flavor a resonance/harmonic state while retaining common broad carrier classes, so a faithful taxonomy **cannot be particle → topology**. The current minimal state is

\[
\boxed{X=(C,F,G,E,B,P)}
\]

for carrier, framing/topology, geometry, excitation, binding, and persistence. The March-2026 Worldlines document actually changes several assignments—including neutrino sector placement and lepton nesting—so it is now explicitly genealogy/context rather than silently overriding the earlier Zoo.

Three additional coded geometry tests passed: near-alignment changes the tangent angle \(73.78^\circ\to32.01^\circ\to7.13^\circ\) without changing interval topology; the short/high-curvature quark-like segment computes cleanly but remains **B-status / topologically unresolved** until endpoint/framing/closure rules are specified; and a bosonic phase ripple can be represented as a normal director field with **exactly zero centerline displacement**, avoiding the accidental assumption that “phase ripple” means a spatially wiggling filament.

The generic three-strand braid also survives numerically: matched-\(z\) separation is \(\sqrt3R_b\), with numerical variation only \(\sim8.9\times10^{-16}\). That establishes the construction, **not** proton/neutron identity.

You’re not wrong—that’s exactly what we need: a dictionary that takes a standard string-mode specification and turns it into a single SAT filament’s transverse vibration (and back again). Here’s a compact, working blueprint.

1) One filament from one string: the core mapping

Pick a single SAT filament embedded as
\mathbf{r}(z,t)=\big(X(z,t),\,Y(z,t),\,z\big),
with z\in[0,L]. We will define X,Y by importing the string’s oscillator content.

Open-string → filament (Neumann at both ends)

Start from the usual open-string mode expansion in conformal gauge (suppressing the center-of-mass and longitudinal pieces, use transverse directions i\in\{x,y\}):
X^{i}(\sigma,\tau)
= x_0^{i} + 2\alpha’ p^{i}\,\tau
	•	i\sqrt{2\alpha’}\sum_{n\neq 0}\frac{1}{n}\,\alpha^{i}_{n}\,e^{-in\tau}\cos(n\sigma).

Set the geometric identification and time reparametrization
\sigma=\frac{\pi z}{L},\qquad \tau=\omega_0\,t,
where \omega_0 is a calibration frequency (see §4). Then define the SAT filament by
X(z,t)=\sum_{n\ge 1}A^{(x)}_n\,\sin\!\frac{n\pi z}{L}\,\cos(n\omega_0 t+\phi^{(x)}n),\quad
Y(z,t)=\sum{n\ge 1}A^{(y)}_n\,\sin\!\frac{n\pi z}{L}\,\cos(n\omega_0 t+\phi^{(y)}_n),
with the amplitude–phase dictionary
A^{(i)}n=\sqrt{2\alpha’}\;\frac{|\alpha^{i}{n}|}{n},\qquad
\phi^{(i)}n=\arg\big(\alpha^{i}{n}\big).
(This is just the real part of the complex mode sum, expressed as sines/cosines with phases. Using \sin vs \cos for the spatial profile corresponds to endpoint convention; Neumann → cos, but with our z\in[0,L] it’s convenient to use \sin and absorb a fixed phase—either is fine so long as it’s consistent.)

Closed-string → filament (periodic)

Closed strings have left/right movers:
X^{i}(\sigma,\tau)=x_0^{i}+ \frac{\alpha’}{2}p^{i}\tau
	•	i\sqrt{\frac{\alpha’}{2}}\sum_{n\neq 0}\frac{1}{n}\Big(\alpha^{i}{n}e^{-in(\tau-\sigma)}+\tilde{\alpha}^{i}{n}e^{-in(\tau+\sigma)}\Big).
Map the loop coordinate to a loop filament (or the same straight filament but with periodic boundary z\sim z+L):
\sigma=\frac{2\pi z}{L},\quad \tau=\omega_0 t,\quad
\Rightarrow\quad
X(z,t)=\sum_{n\ge 1}\Big[ A^{(i)}{n,\mathrm L}\cos\!\big(n(\omega_0 t-\tfrac{2\pi z}{L})+\phi^{(i)}{n,\mathrm L}\big)
	•	A^{(i)}{n,\mathrm R}\cos\!\big(n(\omega_0 t+\tfrac{2\pi z}{L})+\phi^{(i)}{n,\mathrm R}\big)\Big],
with A^{(i)}{n,\mathrm L/R}=\sqrt{\alpha’/2}\,|\alpha^{i}{n}|/n,\,|\tilde\alpha^{i}_{n}|/n and phases from the arguments of the mode coefficients.

That’s the forward map: a standard string state (its \alpha_n,\tilde\alpha_n) picks a unique SAT filament vibration X(z,t),Y(z,t). The timesheet intersections (your fixed/moving dots) are then just slices of this one field \mathbf{r}(z,t).

in the (x,y) plane. This is the ST loop as a record.
	•	Moving timesheet with z-ut=0: the dot is
\gamma_{\text{move}}(t)=\big(X(ut,t),\,Y(ut,t),\,z=ut\big),
giving the 3D trail you visualized.

No extra dof were introduced—the two dots are two foliations of the same worldsheet W=\{(\mathbf{r}(z,t),t)\}.

⸻

3) The inverse map (filament → string quanta → particle)

Given a filament X(z,t),Y(z,t):
	1.	Extract Fourier data. Compute the spatial–temporal Fourier series on [0,L]\times[0,T]:
X(z,t)\approx\sum_{n\ge 1}\Big[a^{(x)}_n\sin\!\frac{n\pi z}{L}\cos(n\omega_0 t)+b^{(x)}_n\sin\!\frac{n\pi z}{L}\sin(n\omega_0 t)\Big],
similarly for Y. Then A^{(x)}_n=\sqrt{(a^{(x)}_n)^2+(b^{(x)}_n)^2}, \phi^{(x)}_n=\arctan2(-b^{(x)}_n,a^{(x)}_n), etc.
	2.	Recover \alpha_n. Use the dictionary

\quad(\text{open}),

\alpha^{i}{n},\tilde\alpha^{i}{n}=\frac{n}{\sqrt{\alpha’/2}}\times(\text{left/right amplitudes}),\ (\text{closed}).

N=\sum_{n\ge 1} n\,\sum_{i}(N^{i}{n,\mathrm L}+N^{i}{n,\mathrm R}),\quad

	•	Take n=1 with \alpha^{x}_{1}\neq 0, others zero.

	•	The fixed timesheet loop is a line segment oscillating in x (ellipse if you also add Y with \pi/2 phase).
	•	Holonomy on that loop sets its charge.

	•	The two “dots” are not extra entities; they’re just two timesheets slicing one worldsheet.

[L2]   "content": "7/3/2026

I'm going to walk you through it verbally, because ^^^ all that stuff, is not SAT. The geometry in my head is SAT. Everything else is LLMs trying to turn it into math, which to my mind shouldn't be that hard, it's just that I can't do the math myself. But mathematics--quite frankly--is *loose*. You can do anything with math, and that's why so many theories go off into lala land, representing and representing, without constraining the way the universe constrains. The universe is very obviously geometric (or at least *every* way in which we have to interact with the universe empirically is, in one way or another geometric). Geometry provides its own constraints. Between the rules of geometry, the grammar of the Minkowski diagram, and the inheritance of extremely detailed system behavior from empirical physics, the pieces are in place for it to be put together in a consistent way. 



The thing we've been lacking is agreement on a consistent language, lack of cognizance of of what sort of language it would have to be, and failure to recognize one simple fact: Particles are the *only* things we observe. Full stop. Particle worldlines, therefore are the nearest thing we have to a map of all of physics, and if done empirically, a particle worldline is unquestionable because to question it would be to question the accuracy of the physical equations that built it, which we know are accurate to great precision. Put a pin in this.



Now... Minkowski really only gives us two things: The worldline, and the timesheet, and those map, essentially, kinematics, so if you know the worldine, you know the kinematics, and vice-versa. And that gives you a lot of basic physics in your diagram. Now, the question arises: What about things that *aren't* kinematics? Well, gravity basically is kinematics, so we're good there [put a pin in this too]. Electromagnetism? Yes, to some extent, there is kinematics involved--Coulomb repulsion is easy enough to diagram, for example. But what about mass, and spin and flavor and color. Well, could go inventing all sorts of other things to put in the diagram, or we could just put a label on the lines, but that's bad theory-making. Occam tells us that. But it's worth mentioning *why*. The reason is that, for each new element you add, you have not just one new way that you can be wrong--in fact, you open up an entire field of possibilities for going wrong... you can run with math just about anywhere you want to go. But we don't generally want to go chasing pretty math just because you can find some set of equations that seem to fit. Not unless there's a clear and obvious connection that makes physical sense *every step of the way*. Plenty of physics drags us through imaginary nonphysical ideas to get where they're going.



We don't. Or, at least, I don't. The way to proceed is to strictly limit yourself to the elements you have until forced to do otherwise by the logic of the system and empirical findings. 



So. The elements we have are the worldline and the timesheet. Are those elements sufficient? The answer is unambiguously yes, provably so. A curve has infinite degrees of freedom, therefore a curve has infinite representational power. Obviously, that means it *must* be possible to encode any empirical data, all of the laws of physics, all of the Presidents' birthdays and favorite songs, and anything else you want to encode. A line can do that simply by choosing an arbitrary encoding language for each sort of information. It's easy to prove that to yourself with a variation on linear representation--can Morse code encode everything? Yes, by virtue of the fact that *language* can encode anything. 



But arbitrary encoding is not ideal, because you then have to encode every piece of information separately. *Geometrically constrained encoding* is what makes this system work. Minkowski already does this for kinematics and gravity. But that doesn't tell us what sort of encoding makes geometric sense for non-kinematic properties. Unless... we assume everything is kinematic. So... is that doable? Let's think about it. Obviously, a lot of things are clearly kinematic... heat, fluid flow, arguably electrical flow... but again, what about *properties* and *forces*? 



Now, here are the two the key insights that make everything else unfold, almost inevitably: 1) because the diagram is constructed to record motion over time, we can examine the diagram to identify what about it specifically encodes motion, and it turns out, it's the angle between the worldline and the time sheet; change that angle, you change the motion and vice versa--this means that *everything* we associate with motion is also necessarily associated with that angle in some way... mass, inertia, trajectory, velocity, acceleration, kinetic energy, gravity, relativistic effects. This gives you what you need to decode (or rather, *encode*) most of physics. 2) NOW we make our first leap. Everything up to now is axiomatic and necessarily true--*if* you make the fairly natural leap of deciding to represent color confinement as a braid of worldines, such that a quark is a triple braid and a meson is a double braid, you now have enough to begin deducing all of the other particle properties. But we'll come back to that. 



First, we should unpack (1) a bit more. We know that angle is associated with velocity by construction; a perpendicular worldline is an object at rest, tilt the angle, increase the velocity, change the worldline orientation. Acceleration is therefore curvature. Want to map a worldline? Just track the way that angle changes with the motion of the timesheet. Or vice versa. For any given motion, there is an instantaneous angle of intersection which measures both the velocity of the object and the angle of intersection; for any change of angle over time, there is a corresponding worldline that uniquely tracks that angle in the topology of its curvature. 



What's more... we made a list of other things that track with motion. Circular motion is an orbit, and that sweeps out a helix in time. Heat is a jitter in the line. Elastic collision is two lines approaching, making contact, and then abruptly changing direction. What else? Well... let's strip down to basics, starting with energy. an object at rest is a straight line perpendicular to the timesheet An object in motion is a straight line at an angle. The worldline of an object with greater mass *curves less sharply* when subjected to a force. These follow from the diagram logic itself, not inserted. Put a pin in this.



Now... what are we going to do about internal degrees of freedom of a particle?  We have two primitives--the worldline and the timesheet. Obviously, particle properties live on the worldline more naturally than on the timesheet. So, we return to the infinite representation capacity of the curve, and we note that these properties are already routinely represented in a way that naturally fits on a curve equation--oscillations. So, we allow the small leap: the curve equation of a worldline must oscillate. Which is to say, that it must be helical. That buys us some options. The intersection with a 3D 'plane' of a helix, extended along the 4-dimensional could be interpreted multiple ways; a simple helix would likely produce a circular trace, and our choice of braiding as the grammar for color confinement gives us two additional intersectional geometries: something like a borromean knot for a hadron, and something like a hopf link for a meson. So, we've got the strong force and color charge already. So, we need spin and flavor. Let us tentatively decide to encode these as nested superhelical coils.   



Now, we don't really have to do that arbitrarily; string theory kind of does that for us, at least in part--because if you look down the barrel of a helix, you see that the intersectional geometry could very easily be represented as an ST vibration mode--so, we just have to collapse ST down to the three-dimensional slice that constitutes our slice. 



Now, we've made three geometrically motivated leaps of logic or represenational choices. We have one more to make. We need to decide what is going on at the intersection. Is the timesheet just passively truncating a portion of the 4D worldline that constitutes the particle that we see? Or is there some *action* here? Let's think about this--if it's passive, then it's a pure formalism, and it cannot have any physical reality; but by the grammar of the diagram, we've already committed to this truncation somehow *instantiating* a particle. Therefore, it *must* be an active boundary. We've already identified, by the logic of the geometry, that geometric parameters... namely, the intersection angle... are associated with velocity, mass, inertia... so let us propose our linchpin: If angle encodes mass (and by f=ma, it must encode force and acceleration as well), then by E=mc^2, that intersection must also encode somehow energy and the speed of light. By the logic of the diagram, the speed of light is already in the motion of the timesheet; thus, c is the speed of *time*.  And there is an energy component associated with the angle, so let us propose that the timesheet exerts a force--that is to say, an energy transfer--upon the worldline, proportional to angle of intersection. This is quite intuitive, as we can think of it almost like friction; a perfectly perpendicular worldline (or a worldine perfectly parallel to the direction of propogation) offers minimum resistance, and thus minimum energy transfer; so, let's measure that angle against the time normal, and say zero degrees is zero energy transfer, and as a worldline approaches 90 degrees (that is, parallel to the timesheet, and perpendicular to the direction of motion), it offers more resistance and picks up more energy.



In this picture, mass is essentially 'time drag'. The long axis of a helical worldline would be the motion vector, but the actual point contact would be the pitch of the helix, or rather (since we're measuring from time normal), the inverse pitch. So, tentatively we can say the actual intersectional angle of particle worldlines approaches 90, and the corresponding resistance is approximately equated to some minimal mass unit--we're going to choose the mass of the electron for reasons I'll get to shortly. 



Now implicit in this picture, we have to consider the fact that we have particles that move at the speed of light, or rather, in our picture, they move at the speed of time... that is, they move with the timesheet, and our energy transfer mechanism makes this natural to interpret as the 'push' of the timesheet. Eg, photons ride worldlines, pushed along by time. This doesn't sound like an extended helical coil necessarily. This sounds like a small excitation. So, let us propose this: A photon is a deviation in a worldline, instantiated as an angular distortion, and carried along as a single oscillation or small packet of oscillations. That fits pretty well. But if that's the case, then other particles that travel at c should be structurally similar. So, now consider what the neutrino might look like in this picture. The neutrino has a measured mass. But if the timesheet exerts pressure upon the kink in the worldline, then by Newton, there must be an equal and opposite force placed upon the timesheet by the particle's kink as well. So, that explains neutrino mass as inertial back-reaction, and the photon must also have such inertial mass, however small. But otherwise they, and other 'massless' particles would seem to fall into a family. Massive particles would be associated with a helical coil, extended long the time axis, while massless particles are small, mobile oscillations pushed by the timesheet. [Put a big pin right here.]



So... let us propose our sixth leap of logic, still strongly geometrically motivated, but now including our energy transfer picture: If the timesheet exerts a force upon the 'kink surface' of the excitation that constitutes our photon or neutrino, propagating that distortion, and that kink has a Newtonian normal force upon the time sheet... then the time sheet--which we've already argued must be a real, active participant--ought to record that force in some way as well. Using the simplest option for how we might represent this, adding the least novel modification to our grammar, we decide that, like the distortion of the worldline, this force manifests as distortion of the timesheet. And let us tentatively suppose then, that a perfectly straight worldline, oriented directly along the axis of time, 0 degrees to the propagation and 90 degrees to the surface, minimal interaction....  that sounds like vacuum. And if our particles are helices, then their local intersection angles are presumably towards the high end, which gives us a lot of room for slightly tilted worldlines to carry--or rather to have imparted upon them--vacuum energy. 



Now, think about that. By trying to follow the minimal logic of Minkowski's existing worldline-timesheet formalism, without manufacturing a single equation, and trying to carefully track our logical leaps so that they are the minimum allowed by the geometric grammar, we've used a system that we *know* is empirically justified and worked through some of the implications of asking that grammar to encode as much of the physical picture as it can. Almost effortlessly, it gives us a mechanism for baryogenesis (or at least mass generation, the genesis of the coiling itself will have to wait), it's given us a mechanism for bosogenesis (or at least 'bosopropagation' in our photon mechanism), it already gives us acceleration and momentum and inertia by construction, it gave us, with just a tiny bit of creativity, color confinement, the strong force (with a very convincing explanation for its strength...if you're trying to pull apart braided worldlines, you're working against the worldlines themselves [implicit in the SAT proposition is that worldlines' physical materiality is extensive across time, but had we not assumed that, then it would have arisen naturally, and necessarily from the braiding proposition]). 



And now, we've constructed by tweak alone, without aiming for it at all, a system where the distortion of worldlines (mass) induces a distortion of the timesheet. And *that*, accidentally lands us exactly where Minkowski started. We have a precise mirror of the metric. Only... it's on the timesheet. But if you think about it... generations of physics students have thought, how weird is it that in GR that mass and motion and space and time are all tangled up. But here we find where GR *actually* lives in the Minkowski model, naturally. If mass distorts the time sheet (literally stretching it against its direction of motion)... then of *course* mass would slow time--the interaction implicit in the Minkowski diagram is already an interaction between mass and *time*, not mass and space. Of course, we've committed to bringing standard science along for the ride... so we recall that space and time *are the same thing*. But let's take that seriously, and since we're minimalists, and we've already made, six I believe, assumptions; I feel like we should reduce our assumption count by saying actually, the minus sign in the Lorenz signature is introducing an unnecessary (and problematic, if you've ever done a Wick rotation) asymmetry. Let us adopt spacetime consistency, call it (++++), assume all of the differences between time and space are unnecessary assumptions except for the one that we can actually witness: It moves differently. Specifically, it has a speed of c and because the 'motion' of space is expansion, then expansion is also the motion of time. Suddenly, time and space *do* look nearly identical. Spacetime is a 4-dimensional manifold, expanding along all axes, mostly at H_0, but at H_0 + c along one axis.

3. Gravitational Perturbations of Relativistic Membranes and Strings
   2022 · Battye, R. A., Carter, B.
   DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.hep-ph/9508300
   Abstract: We consider gravitationally induced perturbations of relativistic Dirac--Goto--Nambu membranes and strings (or {\it p}-branes). We also show how the same equations of motion can be derived from an effective action by a variational principle. Finally, we compare these equations of motion to those using more familiar notation for brane dynamics, which involves the induced metric on the worldsheet. Finally, we compare these equations of motion to those using more familiar notation for brane dynamics, which involves the induced metric on the worldsheet. 8. Gravitational backreaction on a cosmic string: Formalism
   2022 · Chernoff, David F., Flanagan, Eanna E., Wardell, Barry
   DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.1808.08631
   Abstract: We develop a method for computing the linearized gravitational backreaction for Nambu-Goto strings using a fully covariant formalism. We work with equations of motion expressed in terms of a higher dimensional analog of the geodesic equation subject to self-generated forcing terms. The approach allows arbitrary spacetime and worldsheet gauge choices for the background and perturbation. The perturbed spacetime metric may be expressed as an integral over a distributional stress-energy tensor supported on the string worldsheet. By formally integrating out the distribution, this quantity may be re-expressed in terms of an integral over the retarded image of the string. In doing so, one must pay particular attention to contributions that arise from the field point and from non-smooth regions of the string. Then, the gradient of the perturbed metric decomposes into a sum of boundary and bulk terms. The decomposition depends upon the worldsheet coordinates used to describe the string, but the total is independent of those considerations. We illustrate the method with numerical calculations of the self-force at every point on the worldsheet for loops with kinks, cusps and self-intersections using a variety of different coordinate choices. For field points on smooth parts of the worldsheet the self-force is finite. As the field point approaches a kink or cusp the self-force diverges, but is integrable in the sense that the displacement of the worldsheet remains finite. As a consistency check, we verify that the period-averaged flux of energy-momentum at infinity matches the direct work the self-force performs on the string. The methodology can be applied to address many fundamental questions for string loop evolution. 

9. The Evolution of String Theory from a Mathematical Point of View
   2025
   DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.15716136
   Abstract: This review paper explores the evolution of string theory from its origins in hadronic physics to its emergence as a mathematically rich framework with potential implications for fundamental physics. Beginning with the Veneziano amplitude and the dual resonance models, the narrative follows the development of worldsheet conformal field theory, the introduction of supersymmetry, and the intricate web of string dualities. Alongside these physical ideas, the paper highlights the increasing role of mathematics in shaping the theory, focusing on structures such as Lie superalgebras, Calabi-Yau manifolds, modular forms, and topological field theories. Recent developments in category theory, derived geometry, and homological mirror symmetry are presented not as formal embellishments but as conceptual tools that deepen our understanding of the theory’s internal consistency and geometric underpinnings. While the empirical foundations of string theory remain incomplete, its mathematical trajectory continues to illuminate profound connections between physics and modern geometry. 

10. The membrane as a perturbation around string-like configurations
   2022 · Hwang Stephen
   DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.hep-th/0403092
   Abstract: The bosonic membrane in a partial gauge, where one space dimension is eliminated, is formulated as a perturbation theory around an exact free string-like solution. This perturbative regime corresponds to a situation where one of the world-volume space-like dimensions is much greater than the other, so that the membrane has the form of a narrow band or large hoop with string excitations being transverse to the widest dimension. The perturbative equations of motion are studied and solved to first order. Furthermore, it is shown for the open or semi-open cases and to any order in perturbation theory, that one may find canonical transformations that will transform the membrane Hamiltonian into a free string-like Hamiltonian and a boundary Hamiltonian. Thus the membrane dynamics in our perturbation scheme is essentially captured by an interacting boundary theory defined on a two-dimensional world-sheet. A possible implication of this to M-theory is discussed.

papers.abstract: We consider gravitationally induced perturbations of relativistic Dirac--Goto--Nambu membranes and strings (or {\it p}-branes). The dynamics are described by the first and second fundamental tensors, and related curvature tensors in an {\it n}-dimensional spacetime. We show how equations of motion can be derived for the perturbations within a general gauge and then discuss how various simple gauge choices can be used to simplify the equations of motion for specific applications. We also show how the same equations of motion can be derived from an effective action by a variational principle. Finally, we compare these equations of motion to those using more familiar notation for brane dynamics, which involves the induced metric on the worldsheet. This work sets up a general formalism for understanding the effects of backreaction on brane dynamics and the background curvature.
papers.tldr: This study derives equations of motion for gravitationally induced perturbations of relativistic membranes and strings in n-dimensional spacetime, using first and second fundamental tensors, and compares them to familiar notation for brane dynamics.

papers.title: Deformations of extended objects with edges
papers.abstract: We present a manifestly gauge covariant description of fluctuations of a relativistic extended object described by the Dirac-Nambu-Goto action with Dirac-Nambu-Goto loaded edges about a given classical solution. Whereas physical fluctuations of the bulk lie normal to its worldsheet, those on the edge possess an additional component directed into the bulk. These fluctuations couple in a non-trivial way involving the underlying geometrical structures associated with the worldsheet of the object and of its edge. We illustrate the formalism using as an example a string with massive point particles attached to its ends.

papers.title: Strebel differentials and string field theory
papers.abstract: A closed string worldsheet of genus $g$ with $n$ punctures can be presented as a contact interaction in which $n$ semi-infinite cylinders are glued together in a specific way via the Strebel differential on it, if $n\geq1,\ 2g-2+n>0$. We construct a string field theory of closed strings such that all the Feynman diagrams are represented by such contact interactions. In order to do so, we define off-shell amplitudes in the underlying string theory using the combinatorial Fenchel-Nielsen coordinates to describe the moduli space and derive a recursion relation satisfied by them. Utilizing the Fokker-Planck formalism, we construct a string field theory from which the recursion relation can be deduced through the Schwinger-Dyson equation. The Fokker-Planck Hamiltonian consists of kinetic terms and three string interaction terms.
papers.tldr: Strebel differentials and string field theory TLDR: Closed string worldsheets can be presented as contact interactions, and a string field theory is constructed based on this representation.

papers.title: Constructing Spacetime from the String Worldsheet
papers.abstract: In a certain sense riemannian geometry can be thought of as geometry built up from the finslerian properties of point particles. The generalization of this to where the geometry is built up from the finslerian properties of string and membranes is investigated. Solely classical arguments suggest a physical interpretation in which microscopic strings are directly related to macroscopic geometry; alternatively the resulting geometry can be interpretated as that describing microsopic spacetime.
papers.tldr: In this paper, a generalization of riemannian geometry to where the geometry is built up from the finslerian properties of string and membranes is investigated, and the resulting geometry can be interpreted as that describing microsopic spacetime.

papers.title: Gravitational backreaction on a cosmic string: Formalism
papers.abstract: We develop a method for computing the linearized gravitational backreaction for Nambu-Goto strings using a fully covariant formalism. We work with equations of motion expressed in terms of a higher dimensional analog of the geodesic equation subject to self-generated forcing terms. The approach allows arbitrary spacetime and worldsheet gauge choices for the background and perturbation. The perturbed spacetime metric may be expressed as an integral over a distributional stress-energy tensor supported on the string worldsheet. By formally integrating out the distribution, this quantity may be re-expressed in terms of an integral over the retarded image of the string. In doing so, one must pay particular attention to contributions that arise from the field point and from non-smooth regions of the string. Then, the gradient of the perturbed metric decomposes into a sum of boundary and bulk terms. The decomposition depends upon the worldsheet coordinates used to describe the string, but the total is independent of those considerations. We illustrate the method with numerical calculations of the self-force at every point on the worldsheet for loops with kinks, cusps and self-intersections using a variety of different coordinate choices. For field points on smooth parts of the worldsheet the self-force is finite. As the field point approaches a kink or cusp the self-force diverges, but is integrable in the sense that the displacement of the worldsheet remains finite. As a consistency check, we verify that the period-averaged flux of energy-momentum at infinity matches the direct work the self-force performs on the string. The methodology can be applied to address many fundamental questions for string loop evolution.

papers.title: The Evolution of String Theory from a Mathematical Point of View
papers.abstract: This review paper explores the evolution of string theory from its origins in hadronic physics to its emergence as a mathematically rich framework with potential implications for fundamental physics. Beginning with the Veneziano amplitude and the dual resonance models, the narrative follows the development of worldsheet conformal field theory, the introduction of supersymmetry, and the intricate web of string dualities. Alongside these physical ideas, the paper highlights the increasing role of mathematics in shaping the theory, focusing on structures such as Lie superalgebras, Calabi-Yau manifolds, modular forms, and topological field theories. Recent developments in category theory, derived geometry, and homological mirror symmetry are presented not as formal embellishments but as conceptual tools that deepen our understanding of the theory’s internal consistency and geometric underpinnings. While the empirical foundations of string theory remain incomplete, its mathematical trajectory continues to illuminate profound connections between physics and modern geometry.

papers.title: The membrane as a perturbation around string-like configurations
papers.abstract: The bosonic membrane in a partial gauge, where one space dimension is eliminated, is formulated as a perturbation theory around an exact free string-like solution. This perturbative regime corresponds to a situation where one of the world-volume space-like dimensions is much greater than the other, so that the membrane has the form of a narrow band or large hoop with string excitations being transverse to the widest dimension. The perturbative equations of motion are studied and solved to first order. Furthermore, it is shown for the open or semi-open cases and to any order in perturbation theory, that one may find canonical transformations that will transform the membrane Hamiltonian into a free string-like Hamiltonian and a boundary Hamiltonian. Thus the membrane dynamics in our perturbation scheme is essentially captured by an interacting boundary theory defined on a two-dimensional world-sheet. A possible implication of this to M-theory is discussed.

1. The Fokker-Planck formalism for closed bosonic strings
   2022 · Nobuyuki Ishibashi
   Abstract: Every Riemann surface with genus g and n punctures admits a hyperbolic metric, if 2 g − 2 + n > 0 . Such a surface can be decomposed into pairs of pants whose boundaries are geodesics. We construct a string ﬁeld theory for closed bosonic strings based on this pants decomposition. In order to do so, we derive a recursion relation satisﬁed by the oﬀ-shell amplitudes, using the Mirzakhani’s scheme for computing integrals over the moduli space of bordered Riemann surfaces. The recursion relation can be turned into a string ﬁeld theory via the Fokker-Planck formalism. The Fokker-Planck Hamiltonian consists of kinetic terms and three string vertices. Unfortunately, the worldsheet BRST symmetry is not manifest in the theory thus constructed. We will show that the invariance can be made manifest by introducing auxiliary ﬁelds.

2. The Fokker-Planck formalism for closed bosonic strings
   2022 · Martin Lustig
   DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2210.04134
   Abstract: Every Riemann surface with genus $g$ and $n$ punctures admits a hyperbolic metric, if $2g-2+n>0$. Such a surface can be decomposed into pairs of pants whose boundaries are geodesics. We construct a string field theory for closed bosonic strings based on this pants decomposition. In order to do so, we derive a recursion relation satisfied by the off-shell amplitudes, using the Mirzakhani's scheme for computing integrals over the moduli space of bordered Riemann surfaces. The recursion relation can be turned into a string field theory via the Fokker-Planck formalism. The Fokker-Planck Hamiltonian consists of kinetic terms and three string vertices. Unfortunately, the worldsheet BRST symmetry is not manifest in the theory thus constructed. We will show that the invariance can be made manifest by introducing auxiliary fields.

from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

OUT=Path("/mnt/data/meridian_run_146")
OUT.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 1) Guitar-string -> moving-timesheet helix
# u_x+i u_y = A exp[i(k s - omega t)]
# sheet samples s = v_sigma t
# trace angular frequency Omega = k v_sigma - omega
# ------------------------------------------------------------
A=1.0
k=1.0
omega=1.0
v_sheet=0.72
Omega=k*v_sheet-omega
t=np.linspace(0, 8*np.pi/abs(Omega), 1800)
x=A*np.cos(Omega*t)
y=A*np.sin(Omega*t)
q=v_sheet*t

fig=plt.figure(figsize=(7.2,6.0))
ax=fig.add_subplot(111,projection="3d")
ax.plot(x,y,q)
ax.set_xlabel("transverse x")
ax.set_ylabel("transverse y")
ax.set_zlabel("timesheet propagation coordinate q")
ax.set_title("Moving-sheet trace of a straight transversely vibrating filament")
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig(OUT/"guitar_string_timesheet_trace.png",dpi=220)
fig.savefig(OUT/"guitar_string_timesheet_trace.svg")
plt.close(fig)

trace_pitch=2*np.pi*v_sheet/abs(Omega)

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 2) Sheet-flex Green function with tension + bending regularizer
# h(r) proportional to (1-exp(-r/lb))/r
# Pure tension limit h ~ 1/r; force ~ 1/r^2
# Plot dimensionless force magnitude normalized to Newtonian far field.
# ------------------------------------------------------------

**Purpose:** test the minimal geometric consequences of (i) a hypersuperhelical or vibrating filament, (ii) a moving Minkowskian/SAT resolving timesheet, (iii) reciprocal coil↔sheet coupling, and (iv) possible string-worldsheet correspondences.

---

## 0. Source constraints actually used

### Direct/internal
- Nathan's July 2026 `SAT ALL TOGETHER SYNTHESIS.txt`: minimal primitives are worldline/filament + timesheet; angle encodes kinematics; reciprocal force on sheet is an explicit SAT hypothesis.
- `MORE_PYTHON/timesheet_proj.py`: existing "guitar-string with timesheet motion" implementation.
- `🧱SAT ST.txt`: prior SAT↔string oscillator dictionary; useful precursor but not controlling because some boundary-condition statements need repair.
- `WORKSPACES/WORLDTUBE_LAB/FINITE_CORE_TANGENCY_PACKET_002.md`: current local finite-core contact law and the incidence/curvature crossover parameter.
- `CURRENT_HSH_HYPOTHESIS_STATUS_2026-09-14.md`: ᚼ is live SAT solver machinery; Kerr/Kelvin remain live H(s)H hypotheses, but neither is assumed here.

### External comparison
- Akama (1988), *Induced String Action*, DOI 10.1143/PTP.80.935: induced worldsheet actions with intrinsic/extrinsic curvature.
- Battye & Carter (1995), *Gravitational Perturbations of Relativistic Membranes and Strings*, DOI 10.1016/0370-2693(95)00752-7: covariant perturbation/backreaction machinery for strings and membranes.
- Capovilla & Guven (1998), *Deformations of extended objects with edges*, arXiv:math-ph/9804002: coupled bulk/edge fluctuations.
- Ishibashi (2023), closed-string field theory using pants decompositions, DOI 10.1093/ptep/ptad014: pair-of-pants worldsheet topology is standard string-interaction language.
- de Vega & Sanchez (1995), *Classical splitting of fundamental strings*, arXiv:hep-th/9502049: exact classical string splitting solutions.

No external source is being claimed equivalent to SAT/H(s)H.

---

# 1. Minimal geometry

Work in a four-coordinate premetric representation

\[
X^A=(x^1,x^2,x^3,q),
\]

where \(q\) is the SAT propagation coordinate which becomes the Minkowski time-normal direction in the flat readout.

Let the resolving timesheet be the graph

\[
\Sigma_\tau:\qquad
F(X,\tau)=q-c_\Sigma \tau-h(\mathbf x,\tau)=0,
\]

with \(\mathbf x=(x^1,x^2,x^3)\).

The flat Minkowski limit is

\[
h=0,\qquad q=c_\Sigma\tau.
\]

A filament/tube center carrier is

\[
\Gamma(s,\tau)=\bigl(\mathbf u(s,\tau),\,q(s,\tau)\bigr),
\]

with long axis approximately parallel to \(q\).  
A finite-core carrier thickens this by a normal fiber \(K_s\subset N_s\Gamma\).

The observed/readout intersection is the operator

\[
\mathcal I_{\Sigma_\tau}[\Gamma]
=
\Gamma(s_\star,\tau),
\qquad
F(\Gamma(s_\star,\tau),\tau)=0.
\]

This is deliberately separate from the ontology of \(\Gamma\): the trace can be helical even when the material carrier is not.

---

# 2. Hypersuperhelix operator and its relation to a string-mode expansion

A minimal explicit version of one ᚼ nesting step is

\[
\mathcal H_{r,k,\phi,\Pi}[\Gamma](s)
=
\Gamma(s)
+
r\Big[
\cos(ks+\phi)\,N_1(s)
+
\sin(ks+\phi)\,N_2(s)
\Big],
\]

where \(N_1,N_2\) span a selected transported normal plane \(\Pi(s)\).

Recursive hypersuperhelices are

\[
\Gamma_{j+1}=\mathcal H_j[\Gamma_j].
\]

This separates:

- **carrier geometry**: the actual recursively nested path;
- **normal-frame choice**: how each new coil is attached to the previous one;
- **topology/closure**: integer/rational relations among phases and boundary conditions;
- **metric data**: radii, pitches, curvature, torsion.

For small nested amplitudes,

\[
N_a^{(j)}(s)=e_a+O(r_{<j}k_{<j}),
\]

so

\[
\Gamma_N
=
\Gamma_0
+
\sum_j
r_j
\big[
\cos\phi_j\,e_{a_j}
+
\sin\phi_j\,e_{b_j}
\big]
+
O(r_i r_j k_i k_j).
\]

Therefore:

> **Free string-mode superposition is naturally the linearized limit of recursive hypersuperhelix geometry.**

The first nonlinear distinction appears in the moving normal frame. This is the cleanest place to put genuinely H(s)H-specific mode coupling rather than pretending a free Fourier sum and a recursively nested superhelix are exactly the same object.

---

# 3. Exact "guitar-string → helix trace" theorem

Take an almost straight material filament with circularly polarized transverse vibration

\[
u_x(s,\tau)=A\cos(ks-\omega\tau),
\]

\[
u_y(s,\tau)=A\sin(ks-\omega\tau),
\]

\[
q=s.
\]

A flat moving timesheet \(q=v_\Sigma\tau\) samples

\[
s_\star=v_\Sigma\tau.
\]

Hence its intersection trace is

\[
\gamma(\tau)=
\left(
A\cos\Omega\tau,\,
A\sin\Omega\tau,\,
v_\Sigma\tau
\right),
\]

with

\[
\boxed{\Omega=k v_\Sigma-\omega}.
\]

This is exactly a circular helix when \(\Omega\neq0\).

Its pitch per turn is

\[
\boxed{
P_{\rm trace}
=
\frac{2\pi v_\Sigma}{|\Omega|}
=
\frac{2\pi v_\Sigma}{|kv_\Sigma-\omega|}
}.
\]

So a helical particle worldline/readout does **not** logically require a materially helical filament. It can be the moving intersection of a straight vibrating filament with the timesheet.

Generalization:

\[
u_x+i u_y
=
\sum_j A_j
e^{i(k_j s-\omega_j\tau+\phi_j)}
\]

gives

\[
u_{\rm trace}(\tau)
=
\sum_j A_j
e^{i[(k_j v_\Sigma-\omega_j)\tau+\phi_j]}.
\]

Thus the trace frequencies are

\[
\boxed{\Omega_j=k_jv_\Sigma-\omega_j}.
\]

Commensurate \(\Omega_j\) give closed/repeating trace geometry; irrational ratios give quasiperiodic/nonclosing traces.

---

# 4. Does slicing commute with ᚼ?

In general,

\[
\mathcal I_\Sigma\circ\mathcal H
\neq
\mathcal H\circ\mathcal I_\Sigma.
\]

But there is an exact minimal commuting case:

1. flat sheet \(q=v_\Sigma\tau\);
2. ᚼ adds only transverse displacement;
3. ᚼ leaves the longitudinal coordinate \(q=s\) unchanged.

Then \(s_\star=v_\Sigma\tau\) is unchanged by the transform, so slicing and transverse ᚼ mode addition commute.

If ᚼ has a longitudinal component \(\delta q\), or the sheet tilts/flexes, the intersection parameter shifts. Linearizing

\[
F(\Gamma+\delta\Gamma,\tau)=0
\]

gives

\[
\boxed{
\delta s_\star
=
-
\frac{n\cdot\delta\Gamma}
{n\cdot\partial_s\Gamma}
}
\]

for sheet normal \(n\).

This denominator is exactly the incidence factor. It becomes ill-conditioned near tangency and is replaced by the finite-core quadratic-contact law.

This provides the formal bridge between:
- ᚼ nesting,
- timesheet slicing,
- and the existing finite-core tangency program.

---

# 5. Minimal angular coupling

Let \(T\) be the local unit filament tangent and \(n\) the unit timesheet normal.

Define

\[
\mu=n\cdot T=\cos\theta,
\]

where \(\theta=0\) is normal incidence / filament tangent parallel to the sheet normal.

The smallest even, sign-independent resistance function with a minimum at normal incidence is

\[
\boxed{f(\theta)=\sin^2\theta=1-(n\cdot T)^2}.
\]

A local angular interaction energy can therefore begin as

\[
U_\theta
=
\frac{K_\theta}{2}\sin^2\theta.
\]

Its orientational restoring torque has magnitude

\[
\boxed{
|\tau_\theta|
=
K_\theta|\sin\theta\cos\theta|
=
\frac{K_\theta}{2}|\sin2\theta|
}.
\]

Important consequence:

> An angle-only interaction on an exactly flat, homogeneous sheet creates alignment torque, but by itself it does not create a long-range translational force.

A gravitational/Newtonian branch therefore needs an actual sheet deformation field or another nonuniform mediator.

---

# 6. Helix orientation relative to the sheet

For a helix whose local tangent makes internal pitch angle \(\beta\) with its long axis, and whose long axis is tilted by \(\psi\) relative to the sheet normal,

\[
T(\phi)
=
\cos\beta\,a
+
\sin\beta\,e_\perp(\phi).
\]

Averaging around one turn gives

\[
\left\langle(n\cdot T)^2\right\rangle
=
\cos^2\beta\cos^2\psi
+
\frac12\sin^2\beta\sin^2\psi,
\]

hence

\[
\boxed{
\bar f(\beta,\psi)
=
1
-
\cos^2\beta\cos^2\psi
-
\frac12\sin^2\beta\sin^2\psi
}.
\]

Special cases:

\[
\bar f(\beta,0)=\sin^2\beta,
\]

\[
\bar f(\beta,\pi/2)
=
1-\frac12\sin^2\beta.
\]

So both **internal coil pitch** and **axis-to-sheet orientation** influence the mean load.

If a Newtonian/gravitational limit is intended, this orientation dependence cannot remain arbitrary: in the low-velocity weak-field limit it must either be absorbed into the particle's fixed inertial/rest state or average away sufficiently to preserve universality of free fall.

---

# 7. Coil-squash parameter

Use the simple helix

\[
\Gamma(\phi)
=
(R\cos\phi,\,
R\sin\phi,\,
p\phi).
\]

Arc length per radian is

\[
\ell=\sqrt{R^2+p^2}.
\]

If the filament material is approximately inextensible on the squash time scale,

\[
R^2+p^2=\ell^2,
\]

so

\[
\boxed{
R\,\delta R+p\,\delta p=0
}
\]

and therefore

\[
\boxed{
\delta R
=
-\frac{p}{R}\delta p
}.
\]

Axial compression \(\delta p<0\) widens the coil \(\delta R>0\).

Let \(K_{\rm sq}\) be the effective axial pitch stiffness and \(P_c\) the local compressive generalized load from the timesheet. Define

\[
\Pi_{\rm sq}
=
\frac{P_c}{K_{\rm sq}p_0}.
\]

In the small-deformation regime,

\[
\boxed{
S_{\rm coil}
:=
-\frac{\delta p}{p_0}
\approx
\Pi_{\rm sq}\,f(\theta)
}
\]

for the simplest angular loading choice.

This is a **parameterization**, not yet a prediction, because \(K_{\rm sq}\) and the absolute coupling scale have not been derived.

The linear regime requires

\[
\Pi_{\rm sq} f(\theta)\ll1.
\]

Outside it, one must solve the coupled elastic geometry rather than extrapolate the linear squash law.

---

# 8. Sheet flex and the Newtonian limit

Let the timesheet have scalar normal displacement \(h(\mathbf x,t)\).  
Use the smallest isotropic quadratic energy with tension and bending:

\[
E_\Sigma
=

=
\frac{q_i}{4\pi T_\Sigma r}
}.
\]

If another coil couples by \(U_j=-q_j h\), then

\[
\boxed{
\mathbf F_{ij}
=
-
\frac{q_iq_j}{4\pi T_\Sigma}
\frac{\hat{\mathbf r}}{r^2}
}.
\]

This inverse-square law is not inserted manually; it is the Green function of a tension-dominated scalar displacement field living on a **3-dimensional** sheet.

To reproduce Newtonian gravity in the weak-field limit one needs

\[
q_i=\alpha m_i
\]

for the same proportionality \(\alpha\) for all low-velocity test bodies. Then

\[
\boxed{
G
=
\frac{\alpha^2}{4\pi T_\Sigma}
}.
\]

This is a hard consistency condition, not merely a calibration convenience.

It also explains what must be true for the "heavy shock absorber in syrup" intuition to become gravity-like:

- the heavy coil must source a proportionally larger sheet deformation;
- the test coil must also couple proportionally to its inertial mass;
- then \(F\propto m_{\rm source}m_{\rm test}\), so acceleration is independent of the test mass.

A drag force with a fixed friction coefficient does **not** by itself reproduce this.

---

# 9. Short-scale regularization / finite-core limit

With bending stiffness,

\[
\ell_b=\sqrt{\frac{B_\Sigma}{T_\Sigma}}
\]

is the sheet bending crossover scale.

The static Green function becomes

\[
\boxed{
h(r)
=
\frac{q}{4\pi T_\Sigma r}
\left(1-e^{-r/\ell_b}\right)
}.
\]

The force magnitude is

\[
\boxed{
F(r)
=
\frac{|q_1q_2|}{4\pi T_\Sigma r^2}
\left[
1-
\left(1+\frac{r}{\ell_b}\right)e^{-r/\ell_b}
\right]
}.
\]

Thus:

- \(r\gg\ell_b\): ordinary \(1/r^2\);
- \(r\sim\ell_b\): crossover;
- \(r\ll\ell_b\): the point-source divergence is softened;
- a finite \(B^3/B^2/S^2\) carrier smears the source further.

The dynamic long-wave sheet speed is

\[
\boxed{
c_\Sigma=\sqrt{\frac{T_\Sigma}{\rho_\Sigma}}
}.
\]

If this field is intended to represent the gravitational/time-sheet disturbance, the minimal calibration is

\[
c_\Sigma=c,
\]

while \(B_\Sigma\) must be small enough that its \(k^4\) dispersion is below observational limits over tested gravitational-wave scales.

A literal viscosity term \(\eta_\Sigma\) would attenuate waves and define a preferred dissipative medium. That is much harder to reconcile with GR/Lorentz constraints. The syrup analogy is therefore safer as an intuition for **response/damping**, while the Newtonian branch comes from **elastic/tension backreaction**.

---

# 10. Tilted sheet: exact single-trace / multi-trace threshold

Take a static helix

\[
\Gamma(\phi)
=
(R\cos\phi,\,
R\sin\phi,\,
p\phi)
\]

and a tilted moving plane

\[
q-a x=v_\Sigma t,
\qquad
a=\tan\psi.
\]

Intersection requires

\[
p\phi-aR\cos\phi=v_\Sigma t.
\]

The left side is globally monotone if

\[
p>|a|R.
\]

Therefore the moving sheet has exactly one centerline intersection at each time if

\[
\boxed{
|\tan\psi|\frac{R}{p}<1
}.
\]

Since \(R/p=\tan\beta\),

\[
\boxed{
|\tan\psi\,\tan\beta|<1
}
\]

is the exact single-trace condition for this simple helix/plane model.

At

\[
|\tan\psi\,\tan\beta|=1
\]

a fold/tangency appears.

Beyond it, the same sheet can intersect the helix in multiple places.

This is not automatically particle creation; it is a **readout multiplicity transition**.

Near the fold,

\[
\frac{d\phi}{dt}
=
\frac{v_\Sigma}
{p+aR\sin\phi}
\]

becomes large because the intersection point is a kinematic locus rather than a material signal.

For a finite tube/slab, the current finite-core result replaces this singularity by the quadratic contact equation

\[
n\cdot y+\alpha s+\frac12A_{\rm rel}s^2=0
\]

and crossover parameter

\[
\boxed{
\Lambda
=
\frac{|\alpha|}
{\sqrt{|A_{\rm rel}|\rho_{\rm eff}}}
}.
\]

So the exact centerline tilt threshold and the existing finite-core tangency machinery are consistent pieces of the same picture.

---

# 11. Closed-string conjecture: four distinct assignments

## Assignment A — free-string-like vibration field on an almost straight filament

This is the cleanest version of the "guitar string" model.

Require

\[
\partial_\tau^2 u^i
-
c_f^2\partial_s^2u^i
=
0.
\]

For periodic \(s\sim s+L\),

\[
u^i(s,\tau)
=
u_L^i(s-c_f\tau)
+
u_R^i(s+c_f\tau),
\]

which has the same classical left/right decomposition as a free closed-string transverse field after coordinate rescaling.

**What is corresponding:** mode kinematics / wave equation / periodicity.

**What is not yet corresponding:** Polyakov/Nambu-Goto constraints, target-space dimension, quantization, mass-shell relation, gauge charges.

This is a defensible **structural correspondence**, not yet string theory identity.

---

## Assignment B — timesheet intersection trace is "the string"

A moving sheet samples

\[
\gamma(\tau)
=
u(s_\star(\tau),\tau).
\]

If \(\gamma\) closes, one can reparameterize its period as a circle.

But a one-parameter trace cannot generally reconstruct the two-parameter worldsheet \(u(s,\tau)\).

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{
\text{closed trace}
\not\Rightarrow
\text{closed string state}
}
\]

without an additional injectivity/reconstruction assumption.

This is the mathematically weakest literal ST identification.

It can still be useful as an observational projection.

---

## Assignment C — finite tube/support is primary; its sheet section is \(S^1\)

This is the strongest version of "pants, but the spiral on the leg may just be a marking."

For a closed string, a constant-worldsheet-time section is topologically \(S^1\).

A full H(s)H \(B^3\) core intersected by a 3D timesheet generically yields a 3D bulk section (or \(S^2\) boundary section), **not \(S^1\)**.

Therefore an \(S^1\) string-like section requires extra selected structure, for example:

- a rank-two \(B^2\) material support with boundary \(S^1\);
- a distinguished 2D cylindrical sub-surface \(S^1\times I\);
- or an effective boundary mode living on such a sub-support.

This is a powerful discriminator:

> If the closed-string conjecture is literally correct at the intersection level, the H(s)H carrier cannot be only an undifferentiated isotropic \(B^3\) core. It needs a selected string-supporting substructure.

When an \(S^1\) evolves into two \(S^1\) components, the corresponding 2D history has pair-of-pants topology—the standard topological picture of closed-string splitting/joining.

That is a genuine topology match. Dynamics still need to be checked.

---

## Assignment D — material hypersuperhelix itself is the string

Here \(\Gamma_N\) is taken literally as the string embedding.

This requires the strongest conditions:

1. a 2D worldsheet \(X^\mu(\sigma,\tau)\), not only a 1D historical curve;
2. periodic \(\sigma\) for closed strings;
3. Polyakov/Nambu-Goto equations (or a declared effective-string replacement);
4. Virasoro constraints in conformal gauge,
   \[
   (\partial_\tau X\pm\partial_\sigma X)^2=0;
   \]
5. closed-string level matching after quantization;
6. a physically fixed string tension
   \[
   T_s=\frac{1}{2\pi\alpha'};
   \]
7. a target metric/signature map from SAT's premetric or induced geometry to the Lorentzian metric used by the string action.

Without these, "looks like a string vibration" is not the same claim as "is a string-theory state."

---

# 12. Repair to the old SAT↔ST dictionary

The old archive dictionary correctly recognized the usefulness of Fourier mode extraction, but one statement should not be retained:

> Neumann \(\leftrightarrow\cos(n\sigma)\) and Dirichlet \(\leftrightarrow\sin(n\sigma)\) are not interchangeable by an ordinary time-phase shift.

They encode different endpoint conditions.

Also, standard string-theory gauge charges are not obtained merely by declaring the holonomy of an arbitrary projected loop to be \(U(1)\), \(SU(2)\), or \(SU(3)\) charge. Any such SAT assignment requires a separate bundle/compactification/gauge derivation.

---

# 13. Moving timesheet as a chirality-selective sampler

For a free-string-like mode with \(\omega=c_fk\),

co-propagating wave:
\[
u_L\sim e^{i(ks-\omega\tau)}
\]

gives sampled frequency

\[
\Omega_L=k v_\Sigma-\omega,
\]

while the counter-propagating wave

\[
u_R\sim e^{i(ks+\omega\tau)}
\]

gives

\[
\Omega_R=k v_\Sigma+\omega.
\]

If

\[
v_\Sigma=c_f,
\]

then

\[
\boxed{
\Omega_L=0,\qquad
\Omega_R=2\omega
}.
\]

So a sheet moving at the filament wave speed freezes the co-propagating phase and doubles the sampled frequency of the counter-propagating phase.

This is an exact kinematic property of the sampling map.

It is **not yet** an explanation of physical chirality/helicity, but it is important enough to test because a moving SAT timesheet is not a neutral observer of left/right string modes.

---

# 14. What currently survives

## Green
- 🟢 A straight vibrating filament plus moving timesheet exactly produces a helix trace.
- 🟢 Multimode vibration produces a generalized helical/quasiperiodic trace with exact sampled frequencies \(\Omega_j=k_jv_\Sigma-\omega_j\).
- 🟢 ᚼ nesting and timesheet slicing commute in the special flat/transverse case and fail predictably outside it.
- 🟢 Minimal angular coupling gives a clean \(\sin^2\theta\) factor and reciprocal alignment torque.
- 🟢 A 3D sheet-tension field gives a \(1/r\) flex Green function and therefore a \(1/r^2\) two-body force.
- 🟢 Bending stiffness gives a natural short-scale crossover.
- 🟢 Tilted sheet + helix has an exact fold threshold \( |\tan\psi\tan\beta|=1 \).
- 🟢 Finite-core tangency machinery supplies the regularized contact regime near that threshold.
- 🟢 Pair-of-pants topology becomes literal if the primary readout support is an evolving \(S^1\).

## Yellow
- 🟡 Absolute coil squash depends on an un-derived pitch stiffness \(K_{\rm sq}\) and coupling scale.
- 🟡 Newtonian normalization requires a source/load map \(q=\alpha m\) that is not yet derived.
- 🟡 An actual ST correspondence requires a selected \(S^1\) support or a full 2D worldsheet and the string constraints.
- 🟡 Recursive hypersuperhelix geometry agrees with free mode superposition only at linear order unless the operator is specially defined.
- 🟡 "viscosity" is a possible damping analogy, not yet a viable GR replacement.

## Red / do not promote
- ❌ Do not identify a closed one-parameter intersection trace with a complete closed-string state.
- ❌ Do not import ST mass formulas before the Virasoro/level-matching/gauge structure is actually present.
- ❌ Do not claim the scalar sheet-flex model is GR; it currently reproduces only a Newtonian-like Green-function structure.
- ❌ Do not make angle-dependent gravitational mass arbitrary; weak-field universality constrains it severely.

---

# 15. Highest-value next questions

1. **Mass/load map:** Is the SAT inertial quantity derived from coil geometry proportional to the integrated sheet load \(q\)? If yes, Newtonian universality may follow with one coupling constant.
2. **Carrier dimension:** Is the physically privileged finite carrier \(B^3\), \(S^2\), \(B^2\), or layered? Literal closed-string sections strongly prefer an \(S^1\)-supporting substructure.
3. **Constitutive law:** What fixes \(K_{\rm sq}\), \(T_\Sigma\), \(\rho_\Sigma\), and \(B_\Sigma\) from existing SAT/H(s)H geometry rather than by fit?
4. **Metric map:** Can the same \(h\) that gives the Newtonian weak-field potential induce the previously proposed effective Lorentzian metric without contradiction?
5. **Covariance:** Can the sheet equations be written geometrically enough that the preferred resolving foliation is representation/readout rather than an observable Lorentz-violating medium?
6. **String constraints:** Does any current ᚼ-generated two-parameter surface satisfy the Polyakov/Nambu-Goto equations and Virasoro constraints?
7. **Interaction topology:** Can a Three-Spheres / braid / finite-core event generate an \(S^1\to S^1\sqcup S^1\) pair-of-pants history without inserting topology change by hand?
8. **Kerr/ER branch:** Only after the tube/string support is fixed should Kerr/ER be tested as a possible realization; it should not be used to define the geometry retroactively.

script = r'''#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Meridian Run 146: coupled filament-timesheet/string-bridge diagnostics."""
from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

OUT=Path(__file__).resolve().parent

# 1. Guitar string -> moving sheet helix
A=k=omega=1.0
v_sheet=0.72
Omega=k*v_sheet-omega
t=np.linspace(0,8*np.pi/abs(Omega),1800)
x=A*np.cos(Omega*t); y=A*np.sin(Omega*t); q=v_sheet*t
fig=plt.figure(figsize=(7.2,6.0)); ax=fig.add_subplot(111,projection="3d")
ax.plot(x,y,q)
ax.set_xlabel("transverse x"); ax.set_ylabel("transverse y"); ax.set_zlabel("timesheet propagation coordinate q")
ax.set_title("Moving-sheet trace of a straight transversely vibrating filament")
fig.tight_layout(); fig.savefig(OUT/"guitar_string_timesheet_trace.png",dpi=220); fig.savefig(OUT/"guitar_string_timesheet_trace.svg"); plt.close(fig)
trace_pitch=2*np.pi*v_sheet/abs(Omega)

# 2. Sheet flex
lb=1.0
r=np.logspace(-2,2,800); xv=r/lb
Fbar=(1-(1+xv)*np.exp(-xv))/xv**2
Fnewt=1/xv**2
ratio=Fbar/Fnewt
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(7.6,5.2))
ax.loglog(xv,Fbar,label="tension+bending sheet")
ax.loglog(xv,Fnewt,linestyle="--",label="pure 1/r² far-field law")
ax.axvline(1.0,linestyle=":",label="bending scale ℓ_b")
ax.set_xlabel("r / ℓ_b"); ax.set_ylabel("dimensionless force magnitude")
ax.set_title("Sheet-flex force: inverse-square far field with short-scale crossover"); ax.legend()
fig.tight_layout(); fig.savefig(OUT/"sheet_flex_inverse_square_crossover.png",dpi=220); fig.savefig(OUT/"sheet_flex_inverse_square_crossover.svg"); plt.close(fig)

# 3. Mean angle coupling
beta=np.linspace(0,np.deg2rad(89.5),500); psis=np.deg2rad([0,15,30,45,60,75])
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(7.6,5.2))
for psi in psis:
    favg=1-(np.cos(beta)**2*np.cos(psi)**2 + 0.5*np.sin(beta)**2*np.sin(psi)**2)
    ax.plot(np.degrees(beta),favg,label=f"sheet tilt ψ={np.degrees(psi):.0f}°")
ax.set_xlabel("helix tangent angle β to long axis"); ax.set_ylabel("mean angular-resistance factor ⟨sin²θ⟩")
ax.set_title("Orientation dependence of the minimal SAT angular coupling"); ax.legend()
fig.tight_layout(); fig.savefig(OUT/"helix_sheet_angle_coupling.png",dpi=220); fig.savefig(OUT/"helix_sheet_angle_coupling.svg"); plt.close(fig)

# 4. Tilt threshold / root count
R=1.0; p=0.45
phis=np.linspace(-6*np.pi,6*np.pi,8000)
cases=[0.5,1.0,1.5]
bvals=np.linspace(-5,5,301)
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(7.6,5.2))
for mu in cases:
    a=mu*p/R
    f=p*phis-a*R*np.cos(phis)
    counts=[]
    for b in bvals:
        g=f-b
        counts.append(np.count_nonzero(g[:-1]*g[1:]<0))
    ax.plot(bvals,counts,label=f"μ=|tanψ|R/p={mu:g}")
ax.set_xlabel("sheet offset b"); ax.set_ylabel("number of helix-sheet intersections in plotted window")
ax.set_title("Tilt threshold: single-valued trace versus fold/multiple intersections"); ax.legend()
fig.tight_layout(); fig.savefig(OUT/"tilted_sheet_intersection_multiplicity.png",dpi=220); fig.savefig(OUT/"tilted_sheet_intersection_multiplicity.svg"); plt.close(fig)

# 5. Chirality-selective sampling
cf=1.0; vr=np.linspace(0,1.5,500); omega0=cf*k
OmL=np.abs(k*vr-omega0); OmR=np.abs(k*vr+omega0)
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(7.6,5.2))
ax.plot(vr/cf,OmL/omega0,label="co-propagating sampled frequency")
ax.plot(vr/cf,OmR/omega0,label="counter-propagating sampled frequency")
ax.axvline(1.0,linestyle="--",label="v_sheet = c_f")
ax.set_xlabel("v_sheet / c_f"); ax.set_ylabel("|Ω_trace| / ω")
ax.set_title("Moving timesheet acts as a chirality-selective sampler"); ax.legend()
fig.tight_layout(); fig.savefig(OUT/"moving_sheet_chiral_sampling.png",dpi=220); fig.savefig(OUT/"moving_sheet_chiral_sampling.svg"); plt.close(fig)

summary=pd.DataFrame([
    {"quantity":"guitar_trace_Omega","value":Omega,"units":"1/time"},
    {"quantity":"guitar_trace_pitch","value":trace_pitch,"units":"q-units/turn"},
    {"quantity":"sheet_force_ratio_at_r_eq_lb","value":float(ratio[np.argmin(abs(xv-1))]),"units":"fraction of 1/r^2"},
    {"quantity":"tilt_uniqueness_threshold_mu","value":1.0,"units":"dimensionless"},
    {"quantity":"co_propagating_trace_frequency_at_v_eq_cf","value":0.0,"units":"omega"},
    {"quantity":"counter_propagating_trace_frequency_at_v_eq_cf","value":2.0,"units":"omega"},
])
summary.to_csv(OUT/"run146_numeric_summary.csv",index=False)
print(summary.to_string(index=False))
'''
(OUT/"coupled_filament_timesheet_bridge.py").write_text(script,encoding="utf-8")
print(OUT/"coupled_filament_timesheet_bridge.py")
